name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,643

clue.text: It’s money protecting our travel industry

indicators.note: to protect is to guard by wrapping around, so the outer letters surround the inner ones

blocks.note: 'tis is the poetic contraction of 'it is'
M is the abbreviation for money
taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that cash is propping up the country's holiday trade.
explanation.walkthrough: It's must be read as the old poetic contraction, not the modern one, before money's abbreviation is added and the protecting begins after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tourism is the business sector serving holidaymakers and visitors, the commercial side of travel.

clue.text: Drop rent

blocks.note: first meaning: a teardrop, a drop of water from the eye
second meaning: a rip or split in fabric

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the clue looks like an instruction to cut what a tenant pays; rent is really the old noun for a rip, and the two meanings are pronounced differently.
explanation.definitionFit: One word covers both the salty droplet that falls when weeping and a torn split in cloth.

clue.text: Wonderfully skilled peacekeepers preserve city

blocks.note: the United Nations sends peacekeeping forces
to can food is to preserve it in a tin
NY is New York

explanation.surface: Gifted blue-helmeted troops keep a city safe.
explanation.walkthrough: Preserve is a verb in the surface but supplies the tinning sense; New York is the city in its two-letter abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncanny can describe an ability so remarkable it seems beyond normal, as in an uncanny knack.

clue.text: Recess's contents: yellow or colourless fluid

indicators.note: the contents of something are what sits inside its walls, so only the interior letters are kept

blocks.note: a recess is a niche; its inside letters are kept
or is the heraldic name for gold or yellow

explanation.surface: A description of some liquid found in an alcove, either yellowish or clear.
explanation.walkthrough: Recess must be turned into NICHE before its insides are kept. The clue's own 'or' just joins the wordplay to the definition, though it looks like part of a colour choice.
explanation.definitionFit: Ichor is the ethereal liquid said to flow in the veins of Greek gods, and also a thin watery discharge from wounds.

clue.text: Earth thrown up from crumbling hole in works

indicators.note: something crumbling is falling apart, so its letters break up and resettle
one thing placed in another sits inside it, so these letters go within

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a mill is a works or factory

explanation.surface: Spoil heaped up after a hole collapses at a factory site.
explanation.walkthrough: Works means a factory here, giving MILL, and the jumbled hole goes inside it after the M.
explanation.definitionFit: A molehill is the small mound of soil a mole pushes to the surface while digging its tunnels.

clue.text: Many racing cyclists speed ahead, drinking nothing

indicators.note: a drinker takes something inside, so these letters swallow another

blocks.note: to pelt along is to race at speed
O looks like a zero, nothing
to be on or ahead is to be forward

explanation.surface: Riders in a bike race push on hard without taking any refreshment.
explanation.walkthrough: Speed looks like a noun but is the verb, as in pelting down the road; the drinking happens inside the first piece, not the whole.
explanation.definitionFit: The peloton is the main bunched group of riders in a road cycle race such as the Tour de France.

clue.text: Find fault with completely pointless piece by Keats

indicators.note: points are compass letters such as E and S, so being wholly pointless strips every one of them

blocks.note: the word for a part with both its E letters removed
the poet's surname with its E and S removed

explanation.surface: A critic dismissing a poem by Keats as having no point at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Compass points N, E, S and W are the crossword's 'points'; take every one out of PIECE and KEATS to leave PIC and KAT.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick at someone is to nag them with petty criticism, an idiom for carping.

clue.text: Scotch on the rocks? No - dark, sweet stuff

indicators.note: answering no to the word just before it means that word is refused and dropped

blocks.note: a whisky served over ice is liquor on ice

explanation.surface: A bar order is turned down in favour of a dark confection.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotch on the rocks is liquor on ice; the 'No' strikes out the word 'on', leaving LIQUOR plus ICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquorice is a black chewy confection flavoured with the root of a Mediterranean plant.

clue.text: I see through play that's going round in circles

indicators.note: passing through something means being inside it, so these letters sit within
turning round sends the word back the way it came

blocks.note: sport is play or fun
I plus C, the letter that sounds like see

explanation.surface: Someone sees through a drama whose plot goes nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going round in circles' looks like one idiom, but it splits: going round is the signal and circles is the definition. C stands for see by sound.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn are lines of latitude, circles drawn round the globe.

clue.text: Close tight fist around a plotter's heart

indicators.note: to sit around something is to enclose it, so the outer words wrap the inner letters
the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letter is kept

blocks.note: near is an old word for stingy or tight-fisted
taken as written
the central letter of this seven-letter word
a fist is a clenched hand

explanation.surface: A conspirator grips something tightly in a clenched fist.
explanation.walkthrough: Tight fist hints at meanness, which is right for NEAR, but the two words are clued separately and A plus T sit between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something near at hand is within easy reach, nearby, so the phrase is an idiom meaning nearby.

clue.text: Distribute endless Coca-Cola - half is oddly like rum, say

indicators.note: distributing spreads things about, so the letters are scattered into a new order
without ends means the letters at both extremes are cut off
taking things oddly means keeping the first, third, fifth letters and so on

blocks.note: the drink's name with its first and last letters removed
the odd-placed letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Serving cola mixers when half the drink is rum anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' appears twice: the first belongs to the odd-letter fodder, the second links to the definition. The surface hints at rum and Coke; the cola merely supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum is a spirit, so it is an example of something containing alcohol; the 'say' flags rum as one instance.

clue.text: Size limitation's no bar to Shakespeare's general leading army

indicators.note: saying no to something refuses it, so those letters are struck out
to lead is to go in front, so this piece comes first

blocks.note: Banquo is Macbeth's fellow general in the play
a ban is a bar or prohibition, here taken away
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: Rules on size don't stop a Shakespearean commander heading his troops.
explanation.walkthrough: The general is Banquo from Macbeth; a ban is a bar, so removing it leaves QUO, which leads TA, the Territorial Army.
explanation.definitionFit: A quota is a fixed limit on a quantity, such as a maximum amount allowed to be imported or caught.

clue.text: Where Charlotte lies, with Virginia lying on top?

definitions.text: Where Charlotte lies, with Virginia lying on top?

blocks.clueFragment: Where Charlotte lies, with Virginia lying on top?
blocks.note: surface reading: a racy scene with two women, one lying on the other

blocks.clueFragment: Where Charlotte lies, with Virginia lying on top?
blocks.note: setter's reading: Charlotte is a big US city and Virginia a state bordering its state to the north

explanation.surface: Two women, Charlotte and Virginia, in a compromising position.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlotte and Virginia look like women's names; they are a city and a neighbouring state, and on top means to the north on a map.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte is the largest city in this southeastern US state, and Virginia sits directly above it on the map.

clue.text: One stopping riot, perhaps, left with loot

blocks.note: spoils are plunder or loot
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A policeman breaking up a riot gets away with stolen goods.
explanation.walkthrough: Riot here is a riot of fun, an uproarious good time, not civil disorder; the 'perhaps' marks it as one example of the fun being ended.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoilsport ruins other people's enjoyment, so ending a riotous good time is typical of one.

clue.text: Bawling, losing head and interrupting row in intrusive manner

indicators.note: losing the head means the first letter is cut away
to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so these letters go inside

blocks.note: crying, with its first letter dropped
to ply is to row or work a boat back and forth

explanation.surface: Someone loses their temper shouting at a meddler in a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: Row suggests a quarrel, but it is the boating verb, matched by PLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Pryingly describes acting nosily, poking into others' private affairs, which is what intrusive behaviour does.

clue.text: Mister Lee Burn is mistaken

indicators.note: being mistaken is being wrong, so the letters stand in the wrong order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Mr Lee Burn has got something wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Mister looks like the title of a man; read it as one that makes a mist. The 'is' does double duty as fodder and as part of the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A nebuliser turns liquid medicine into a fine spray for inhaling, so it is literally a device that produces mist.

clue.text: Trashy hotel to stick around

indicators.note: moved around means the letters are shifted into another order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
H is hotel in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A tacky hotel that one is told to hang about in.
explanation.walkthrough: Stick around looks like 'stay', but around works on the word before it, and the H for hotel goes at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Kitsch is used of art or decor in garish poor taste, so it serves as a label for trashy things.

clue.text: Discovering singular sign of discontent?

blocks.note: first meaning: finding out someone's secret, an informal British sense
second meaning: a murmur of complaint, here in the singular

explanation.walkthrough: Rumble in British slang means to see through or find out someone, as in 'we've been rumbled'. The second sense is usually plural, which is why the clue says singular.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both catching someone out and a low growl of grumbling unrest among a group.

clue.text: During climb, I begin to drink

indicators.note: during means within the span of something, so the letters lie inside the following words

blocks.note: letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: A climber starts on the bottle partway up.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the end of climb through I into the start of begin.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbibe is a formal or humorous verb for consuming alcohol or any liquid.

clue.text: UK native heard the French can be sensitive

indicators.note: what is heard is only the sound, so the spelling may differ

blocks.note: a Brit is a British person
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A Briton overhearing French gets touchy.
explanation.walkthrough: Brit gains its double T only through sound, so heard applies to the first part alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Brittle temperaments are easily upset or fragile, so the word can mean touchy or easily hurt.

clue.text: Reeve's role, originally, over staff

blocks.note: super- is the prefix meaning over or above
to staff is to man a post

explanation.surface: A medieval reeve's job was first to supervise the workers.
explanation.walkthrough: Reeve suggests an old English steward, but it is Christopher Reeve, star of the 1978 film; 'originally' because later actors took the part.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Reeve was the first big-screen star of the modern superhero films, playing the caped hero.

clue.text: Setter originally served eggs flipped in Army cookware

indicators.note: something's origin is its start, so only the opening letter is kept
flipping something over turns it end to end

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as me
the first letter of the word
nits are the eggs of lice

explanation.surface: A cook serves eggs flipped in a soldier's pan.
explanation.walkthrough: Eggs suggest breakfast, but they are lice eggs, NITS, which flip to STIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess tin is the metal dish soldiers cook and eat from in the field, named after the military mess.

clue.text: Return handwritten document, enclosing ring, as greeting

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the letters run the opposite way
to enclose is to surround, so these letters wrap around another piece

blocks.note: MS is the abbreviation for manuscript
a halo is a ring of light

explanation.surface: Sending back a letter with a ring inside it as a greeting.
explanation.walkthrough: Manuscript literally means written by hand, so the familiar abbreviation fits; return applies to that abbreviation before it does the enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Shalom is the Hebrew word for peace, used as a greeting both on meeting and parting.

clue.text: Fall badly beneath shower head and squeal

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters are set in a wrong order
the head of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept

blocks.note: a spill is a fall, as from a horse or bike
taken as written, to be rearranged
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone slips under the shower and lets out a shriek.
explanation.walkthrough: Fall badly reads as one phrase, but badly works on the words after it. Squeal is the informer's slang, not a cry of pain.
explanation.definitionFit: To spill the beans is an idiom for revealing a secret, and to squeal is slang for informing on someone.

clue.text: Don't apply to O2 for one

blocks.note: do in the sense of be, as in 'these rules do not apply'
N/A, not applicable, is what a form says when a question does not apply

explanation.surface: A warning not to send an application to a mobile phone company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't apply' is read as 'are N/A', not applicable. The O2 is a large indoor venue in London, and O2 is also a British mobile network.
explanation.definitionFit: The O2 is a famous London entertainment venue, so it is an example of a large indoor arena.

clue.text: Fragment of molar on back of mouth

indicators.note: a fragment is a small broken-off part, so the letters come from inside the words
going back means running the other way

blocks.note: letters from these words read backwards

explanation.surface: A piece of tooth breaks off at the back of the jaw.
explanation.walkthrough: Back of mouth looks like a location in the jaw, but back is the signal and 'of mouth' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Oral is the adjective for anything relating to or done by the lips and tongue, as in oral hygiene.

clue.text: Curses musketeer over being posted to front

indicators.note: being sent to the front means a letter leaves its place in the word and is put at the start

blocks.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for an over
Athos, one of Dumas's Three Musketeers, with its O lifted out

explanation.surface: A musketeer swears at being sent to the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: The O already in ATHOS moves to the front, giving O-ATHS.
explanation.definitionFit: Oaths are swear words, so curses fits as a plural noun for profanities.

clue.text: Legendary horseman familiarly talked of racecourse here

indicators.note: what is talked of is spoken, so its sound counts rather than its spelling

blocks.note: Lester Piggott, the great jockey, known by his first name

explanation.surface: A famous rider is mentioned in connection with a racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: Lester Piggott was Britain's most celebrated jockey, hence 'familiarly'. The English city is pronounced like his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Leicester is an English Midlands city with its own horse-racing track, so a racecourse is found there.

clue.text: Article on maths initially covering old formula

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so just the first letter is kept
to cover something is to go around it, so outer letters enclose inner ones

blocks.note: the definite article
O is the abbreviation for old
re means on or concerning
the word's opening letter

explanation.surface: A piece of writing about maths that discusses an old formula.
explanation.walkthrough: Re is the crossword's 'on', as in 'regarding'. The article and the first letter of maths stay together as the outer shell.
explanation.definitionFit: A theorem is a proven mathematical statement, often expressed as a formula or rule.

clue.text: Mistress Gwyn doesn’t finish fruit, cut beforehand with hooked implement

indicators.note: not finishing means stopping short of the last letter
cutting trims off the final letter
coming beforehand means being placed earlier, so this piece goes first

blocks.note: grape with its last letter cut
Nell Gwyn, Charles II's mistress, minus the final L

explanation.surface: Charles II's mistress leaves fruit half-eaten, earlier sliced with a hook.
explanation.walkthrough: Nell Gwyn was an actress and royal mistress famous for selling oranges; 'beforehand' puts the fruit first.
explanation.definitionFit: A grapnel is a small anchor or grappling iron with several hooks, used for catching hold.
